en: *The Profound Meaning Record of the Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara*, Collated Edition, Volume One.
*Record of the Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara*, Volume One.
Narrated by the Song Dynasty Shramana Zhili of Siming.
Zhi Li bows low and reflects: in my youth, when I aspired to study, I entered the Baoyun Monastery and encountered Master Shoufashi, who expounded this chapter for me.
As my spiritual faculties were dull, I repeatedly consulted him regarding my doubts. My former teacher, mindful of my diligent studies, did not decline to instruct me personally;
thus, the meanings he explained I have roughly committed to memory. Those who formerly heard the teaching together with me are now each in their decline, and I fear...

May those with foresight find benefit therein, and may future generations strive together for their own lack of talent. I have transcribed this for the world, yet fearing my own dull intellect and ignorance, there may be errors in what has been transmitted;

it is my hope that the sages of the Perfect School (Yuanzong) will correct it. This preface was completed on the first day of the eighth month in the year Wuxu (the fifth year of the Tianxi era). Thus ends the introduction.
The Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara, Volume One.
This *Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara* is presented here in brief; its full title should be *The Profound Meaning of the Universal Gate Chapter of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara*.
It is abbreviated because both the introduction and the main text clearly elucidate both the person and the Dharma.

Regarding the term "Profound Meaning" (*xuanyi*): it refers to the categories of meaning that can explain [the text]. "Profound" (*xuan*) is a designation for that which is obscure, subtle, and difficult to perceive;

"meaning" (*yi*) signifies that there is a deep underlying reason. This is because the Great Master, through the power of samādhi, penetrated the limit of the Dharma-nature and deeply perceived the intent regarding persons and dharmas in this chapter.
One should know that the five meanings, beginning with "name," are all entirely obscure and subtle. 7.
Regarding the title *Upāyapuruṣajñānadarśana*, Volume One: since there are two fascicles, they are distinguished as "Upper" and "Lower.
Next, the person who can expound [this teaching] is shown.
The Master Zhiyi of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty spoke [these words];
since these were recorded by his disciples, they did not dare directly mention his dharma-name.
Mount Tiantai is the place where the Master resided and entered parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is referred to by this name.
The location reveals the person; it is named after the mountain where he resided and entered parinirvāṇa.

The details regarding his physical appearance at the time of death and the spiritual wonders that followed his passing are fully contained in the *Daben* (Great Text), the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice), and the *Biezhuang* (Separate Biography); they are not recorded here in full.

As for "Zhizhe" (the Wise One), this refers to the Emperor of the Sui dynasty, who requested to receive the Bodhisattva Great Precepts. Upon its completion, the Master said: "Your Majesty has traveled far to follow the Sage."

The Master Jin (Jin Yi) styled himself "Dhāraṇī-rāja" (Total-Holding King). The *Dìchí jīng* (Earth-Holding Sūtra) states that transmitting the lamp of the Buddha-dharma is precisely what defines a teacher of wisdom (*jñānin*).

Since he had transmitted the lamp, he was thereafter styled "Zhìzhě" (Wisdom-Knower). From then on, in all his memorials and correspondence, he referred to himself as "the disciple Dhāraṇī, with humble greetings.
As for the term "Dàshī" (Great Master), this is a title used for emperors and great personages whom one serves; therefore, it was so designated.
This is not like the titles used today for those appointed to office, which are intended merely to please the speaker;

nor is it like the flowery rhetoric of those who delight in eloquent discourse to satisfy their own refined inclinations—unlike other masters who collect from the sūtras and śāstras to compose commentaries and sub-commentaries for the purpose of explaining the scriptural texts.
Thus, when Dharma Master Darien saw Zhizhe expounding the Dharma before the assembly, he sighed and said: "This is not [mere] literary composition."
What is recorded in the Commentary is that one observes the capacities of beings and employs eloquence as appropriate: Prajñā is neither dull nor sharp;

its sharpness or dullness arises from the abundance of conditions suited to the time—this is the mark of sharpness. When the pond is deep and the flowers large, the dull-witted may attain it with ease.

The record of the disciple Guanding’s memorialization of the Master’s life is fully manifest in the *Benzhuan* (Biography), which details the beginning and end of the Venerable Zhāng’ān’s spiritual practices and miraculous manifestations. The commentary on the text is divided into two parts:

first, an explanation of the preface; second, [the explanation of the main text]. Within the first part, there is an account of how the True and the Responsive benefit sentient beings; within that, the first section provides a direct clarification.

Regarding the first of the two [sections on] the True and Responsive bodies, there are three parts: first, demonstrating the wondrous function of the two bodies; second, clarifying that because the essence is wondrous, its functions vanish;
third, within the first [of these], showing how phenomena merge so that the responsive vanishes.
Now, the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, such that there is no image to be imaged.

The perfect interfusion of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) means that because form and mind, as well as the environment and its inhabitants, are identical to their true nature, a single phenomenon encompasses all phenomena, and likewise, all phenomena encompass a single one. Thus, every phenomenon universally pervades every other without boundary or limit;
it is precisely through the absence of boundaries that this constitutes its realm. This Dharma-realm is entirely interfused, encompassing the hundred realms and the thousandfold world.
Just as it is with a hundred or a thousand worlds, one may therefore say that there is only form, only mind, only the basis, and only the manifest.
Were it otherwise, it would not be perfect interfusion. Avalokiteśvara realizes this as his fundamental essence and, based upon this wondrous essence, gives rise to responsive manifestations.
He responds to the capacities of beings within the Dharma-realm by means of the Dharma-realm; likewise, he is moved by the capacities of beings within the Dharma-realm.

The Dharma-realm corresponds to the Dharma-realm; there is no duality of subject and object, and they are naturally forgotten. If even the resonance and response are forgotten, how could essence and function be different?
Therefore, although a response is manifested, no response exists that can be maintained; thus it is said that the image has nothing to which it corresponds.
Second, regarding the nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) being pure and truly forgotten:
true suchness is pure, and thus there is nothing to transform in its transformation.
As for the purity of true suchness, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "True suchness refers to the mind-nature, which is neither born nor extinguished."

Because it is extinguished, all dharmas from the very beginning are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects;
they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible. Being solely this one mind, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness).
Furthermore, it is said that the essence of this *tathatā* has nothing that can be discarded, because all dharmas are entirely...
Since all are true, there is likewise nothing that can be established, for all dharmas are identical to suchness (*tathatā*).

Since neither refutation nor establishment is possible, one cuts off speech and thought; thus, they are fundamentally non-correspondent with the *saṃsāric* afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Therefore, it is called "Pure.
Avalokiteśvara realizes this as his fundamental essence and manifests this very essence to all sentient beings, causing them to engage in contemplative practice.
If one possesses the knowledge or the semblance of insight that perceives this, such a knower and seer achieves the benefit of subduing and severing [afflictions].

If one does not yet possess this knowledge and insight, yet is able to apply diligence through the three karmas to become a fit vessel and thereby escape all suffering, they are also called "transformed" (*nirmāṇa*).

These are all manifestations of the True Body (*dharmakāya*) benefiting sentient beings. Question: Regarding the shared object of perception, why are these two types termed "response" (*nairmāṇika*) and "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*)? Answer: They are so named because of their respective modes of appearance.

Question: Since all bodies are not bodies of wisdom-virtue (*jñānaguṇa*), how is it that they are now transformed into the true body (*dharmakāya*)? Answer: Transformation that occurs suddenly is "transformation-manifestation" (*nirmāṇanirmita*).
Here, in contrast to the discussion of images, "transformation" refers to "transformative transformation" (*pariṇāmika-nirmita*). Why is this so?

Because the previous statement regarding images included all responsive transformations as being images, and from one's own true retribution body down to the bodies in other hells, all were already subsumed.
If you wish to transform ordinary beings and sages and lead them into sainthood, you must manifest true wisdom; if it were not the True Body, transformation would be impossible.
To say that there is no one to be transformed when speaking of transformation means that, based on the equality of nature, one forgets the merit of the act of transforming.
Although one causes those in the nine realms to all proceed toward nirvana, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction; this is the Buddha of the Equal and True Dharma-realm.
Not delivering sentient beings, yet transforming them all day long; though transforming them all day long, there is no transformation.
Second, although it resembles the mundane, it clarifies that because the function is forgotten, the two benefits are pervasive. First, it reveals the pervasiveness of the benefit.
Although the image has nothing that is being imaged, there is nothing that it does not image.

Although all phenomena of form and mind have no nature of arising, they arise as such by the convergence of causes and conditions. The wondrous realization of Avalokiteśvara is identical to the nature of all phenomena;
although it is without form or appearance, when struck by the various capacities of sentient beings, there is no image that does not manifest. This is due to...
Because it is free from the thought of responding to specific conditions, it is able to respond universally to the myriad capacities within the Dharma-realm;
it is like a bright mirror that manifests images without conceptualization, and thus it is said that there is nowhere it does not reflect.
Second, transformation is without lower obscurity and its benefit is universal.
There is nothing that is not transformed by this transformation;
yet, although the preceding words permeate the beginning of this phrase, in its actual nature, it is neither subject to change nor does it transform.

The transformation between delusion and awakening is manifest; Avalokiteśvara accords with principle, and though he knows that all is unchanging, he constantly employs true wisdom to transform all ordinary beings, such that they become non-dual sages.
This is because he is free from the thought of transforming beings; thus, he causes others everywhere to change their delusion into awakening.
It is like a magnet that attracts without intention; therefore, it is said that there is nowhere he does not transform.

Third, because there is no lower obstruction, the mutual manifestation of the two bodies is established; this has two parts. First, regarding the characteristics of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body):
therefore, it neither exists nor does not exist, as the transformation and enjoyment bodies manifest throughout the nine realms of existence.

Because the Middle Way Dharma-realm simultaneously negates both extremes, it has no fixed location; because it simultaneously illuminates both aspects within its own essence, there is nowhere it does not exist.
Regarding the manifestation of bodies that respond to the nine realms of existence, this text states: "Manifesting transformation means sudden appearance.

This interpretation, along with the inclusion of "responding," establishes two aspects and fully manifests the characteristics of beneficial activity. Question: The Sūtra says, "If one should be saved by a Buddha-body, he immediately manifests a Buddha-body. How is this understood?
Now, as for the question of why it is said there are nine: regarding the body of the Buddha-realm, there is both the universal and the restricted.
The restricted refers to the body of the marks of wisdom of the Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue), wherein the three thousand realms of reality are fully exhausted;

since even this is not seen by the eye-mind of the Equal Enlightenment (Dengjue), how much less so by those of lower stages or ordinary and Hinayana practitioners? The universal, however, includes the marks at the stage of fruition in the three teachings, as well as those of the Perfect Teaching.
Although the visions of ordinary beings and sages differ in being coarse or subtle, all are called the Buddha-body; however, these are manifestations appearing according to the capacities of beings.

Because they are what is seen by the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (empirical consciousness) or the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness), although they are the Buddha-body, they are generally subsumed within the realms of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas.
The scriptural passage speaks of "manifesting ten" from a general perspective, whereas the present text speaks from a specific perspective.
It is said that among the nine paths,
two locations possess the virtue of the lower true body;
these locations contain the passage on the non-permanence of existence and the entry into the non-duality of quiescence.
Generally, the nine realms are designated as "existence" because they all possess karmic retribution.

Although the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) dwells within them, its true wisdom is inherently merged with the ultimate principle; thus, it is said that it "quiescently enters" the principle of non-duality.
The former [refers to] manifesting responsive forms while remaining the True Body (dharmakāya); this [refers to] revealing the True Body while remaining the responsive form.
Second, the following clarifies the two functions for gathering and sustaining living beings (*saṃgraha-vastu*).

Thus, by means of the three karmas, one petitions [the Buddhas] so that they may grant liberation from the shores of suffering; through the Four Great Vows, one ensures that all may partake in supreme bliss.

Having thus clarified above the two functions of the True and the Responsive, the first two phrases now demonstrate the aspects of bestowing and uprooting in the gathering and sustaining of living beings.
The first two lines clarify the True Body (dharmakāya) as it uproots suffering; the subsequent two lines demonstrate the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) as it bestows bliss.

The Buddha answers the former question by showing how the three karmas manifest as a response to the latent capacity of the seeker, such that the seven calamities, the two types of seeking, and the three poisons are all exhausted at the limit of suffering;

thus it is said they "receive liberation from the precipice of suffering. The Buddha answers the latter question by showing how the three karmas respond to the latent capacity of the seeker across the three lands.
Because sentient beings obtain tenfold benefits that ultimately lead back to the secret treasury, it is said that they are made to partake in supreme bliss.
However, these four vows do not exclusively bestow bliss; although they are clarified here, they actually pervade the preceding phrase.

Since the three types of karma above are precisely what can evoke [the response], this clarification of the four vows constitutes the basis for that responsive capacity. Thus, the upper and lower sections mutually illuminate one another, such that neither is lacking.
One should know that the three karmas also pertain to the hidden potential (*míngjī*); although they do not exist in the present, one must possess them from past lives.
Thus, the second section below clarifies both the fundamental and the manifested aspects. First, it demonstrates the various names. First, the names of causes in the present and the past.
Therefore, in the Sahā world, he received the name "Fearless" from the Buddha Ratnagarbha and was granted the title "Avalokiteśvara.
Now, in this Land of Endurance (*Sahā-lokadhātu*), those who are called "Fearless" appear twice in this sutra amidst the perils of hostile robbers; in one instance, a person cries out:
"O sons of good family, do not be afraid! You should with one mind invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara."

Regarding the name, it is said that this Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings, even to the point of stating that by merely invoking his name, one immediately attains liberation.
Furthermore, within the section on exhorting offerings, the Buddha himself praises him, saying:
"This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terror and urgent distress; for this reason, in this Sahā world..."
In all worlds, he is universally known as the Bestower of Fearlessness (Abhayamdada). Regarding those such as Ratnagarbha and others, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"In the past, during the Kalpa of Sustained Virtue (Sudhara) in the world-system of Saṃdṛśa, there appeared a Buddha named Ratnagarbha.
At that time, there was a wheel-turning king named Anantanetra whose eldest son, for three months, made offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus."

When I resolve upon the Bodhicitta, if there are sentient beings who undergo all manner of suffering and affliction in the three miserable realms, and if they can mindfully remember me and invoke my name—should they not be relieved from their suffering as perceived by my celestial ear and celestial eye, may I never attain supreme, precious enlightenment.
The Buddha said: "Observe all sentient beings; you wish to sever the [suffering] of all..."
Because of this suffering, I now bestow upon you the name Avalokiteśvara.
Second, although you have already attained the title of "Awakened One" (Buddha), it is not yet the designation for one who has completed the task;
you have already achieved the title of "Seed-Awakened One" (Bodhisattva) as Samantabhadra, and next, when you are to succeed [to Buddhahood], you shall be called Samantaraśmiguṇa.
Regarding those who have already attained [Buddhahood], the *Sūtra of the Great Compassionate One with a Thousand Hands and Eyes* states:

"The inconceivable power of the majestic spiritual authority of this Bodhisattva has already resulted in his becoming a Buddha in the past during immeasurable kalpas; his name was Tathāgata Saddharmaprabhāsa (Tathāgata of the Radiance of the True Dharma).
Yet, through the power of his great compassionate vows to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, he manifests as a Bodhisattva. Furthermore, the *Avalokiteśvara...* [text continues].
The *Mèijīng* (Sutra on the Profound Meaning) states: "He had already attained Buddhahood previously, titled Tathāgata Righteous Dharma Radiance (*Zhèngfǎmíng Rúlái*);

Śākyamuni was his disciple who practiced asceticism under him. Regarding the phrase "next shall [attain it] as equal [to him]," the *Guānshìyīn Shòujì Jīng* (Sutra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara) states:

"Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara shall next attain perfect enlightenment after Amitābha; he shall be named Tathāgata Universal Radiance Merit Mountain King (*Pǔguāng Gōngdé Shānwáng Rúlái*) and shall succeed him."
The term "dwelling" (chu) is analogous to the meaning of a "heir apparent" (chujun).
Its dual fundamental nature and its downward connection are difficult to fathom.
Since its essence and manifestations are such as this, how could they be measured or known? It is merely a single name raised according to conditions through skillful means.
As stated in the aforementioned sutras, some have already attained the state of Tathāgata, while others manifest as Bodhisattvas;
in past worlds, they served as teachers of Śākyamuni during the True Dharma, and today Avalokiteśvara still occupies the place of Amitābha.

Furthermore, just as Mañjuśrī was originally the ninth-generation patriarch of the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni), such that the descendant has already perfected the fruit while the ancestor remains at the stage of cause—their fundamental and manifested traces are thus sublime.
The lower section may be measured, yet it must employ the four phrases of high and low to manifest the inconceivable characteristics of the various sages.

Second, the current discussion of "the lower" provides a title for the persons and the Dharma; first, the description of the persons, which includes the word "scripture. First, the description [of the persons].
Regarding the first of these two names for the person,

it was translated from the Sanskrit as "Brahmā" (Fan). The name now given as Guanshiyin is the correct transliteration of the Western land's original sound, *Avalokiteśvara*, which means "Observer of the World’s Sounds."

In various *dhāraṇī* sūtras, the original Sanskrit name was first cited, while the Chinese transliteration has since become somewhat abbreviated; furthermore, the Chinese translations of the name appear in various forms.

Some call him Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara), others call him Guanzizai (Avalokitasvāmī). Only in the *Qianshouqianyan Dabeijing* (The Sūtra of the Thousand Hands and Eyes of Great Compassion) is he called "Guanshiyin Zizai Pusa" (Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara);
this meaning seems sufficient, yet the distinction is clarified by considering the relationship between the object (*viṣaya*) and the wisdom (*jñāna*).

If one follows the present [explanation], the three characters [of the title] manifest their meaning without deficiency; according to the current interpretation, they already reveal sovereign mastery.

Second, regarding the "subject and object" section, the meaning is explained by means of the *Huayan* (Flower Ornament) Sūtra. This has two parts: first, the individual explanations; second, the initial explanation. First, the explanation of the character "contemplation" (*guan*).
Within this, there is the subtle and thorough penetration of the Middle Way and the extremes.
The subject and object are perfectly interfused, and existence and non-existence are both fully realized.
Within this perfect interfusion of subject and object lies the wisdom of the Middle Way; within this full realization of existence and non-existence lie the two wisdoms.

It is solely within a single mind that there is simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination. At the very moment of illumination, one penetrates the Two Truths; thus it is said they are "both fully realized. This, then, is the ten realms.
The sounds of speech arise as they are observed, constantly obstructing and constantly illuminating.

These two illuminations exhaustively penetrate the lower [levels] so that both the cultivated nature (*bhāvanā-dhātu*) and the innate nature (*prakṛti-dhātu*) are clarified. Because this illumination exhaustively penetrates the true nature (*dharmatā*) and examines its beginning and end, it is called "observation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Illuminating the ultimate reaches reveals the nature of inherent virtue; examining its beginning and end reveals the virtue of cultivation.

This is based on the wondrous object to manifest the wondrous wisdom that the three thousand realms are inherently complete. Although these correspond to the three truths, because they are contrasted with the aspect of cultivation, they are here combined and referred to simply as "the nature of reality" (*dharmatā*).

Within the stage of cultivation, the conditions of *pratyaya* (enabling) and *hetu* (causal) each have their own beginning and end. Joining the palms and bowing the head is the beginning of the condition of *pratyaya*; it is merit.
The adornment of virtue is the end of the causal stage; a single phrase or a single verse is the essence of the realized stage. The adornment of wisdom is the end of the realized stage.

If this is so for practice in accordance with the truth, it is likewise for practice in opposition to it. At the time of committing evil, how could the mental factor of wisdom and the various other factors not be its essence?
At the time of undergoing suffering, the habitual fruit and the retributive fruit are precisely its end. If one considers this...

The principles of cultivation and nature reach their ultimate point in the meaning of their beginning and end. Only when speaking of the fundamental nature can the three thousand virtues be fully exhausted;

only when discussing the culmination of cultivation can the arising of the three thousand be thoroughly investigated. No wisdom higher than these three can illuminate this realm, and no wondrous realm other than this can give rise to that wisdom.
They may be compared to a box and its lid, or water and milk.
Second, the explanation of "Avalokiteśvara" (World-Hearing).
"World-Hearing" refers to the object of contemplation. Myriad phenomena flow and change, separated and distinct;
though their voices cry out differently, all alike receive liberation from suffering.
The sounds of the sentient beings of the ten realms crying out for help when encountering suffering and invoking the Name—these are the objects of contemplation.

While the aforementioned objects and wisdom are both the "contemplating subject" and can be compared to a hammer and an anvil, this World-Sound (Avalokiteśvara) may be compared to the raw material itself.
By contemplating this World-Sound, one causes those in the ten realms to all be liberated from the three obstacles. Furthermore...
One should know that the preceding object and wisdom are precisely the inconceivable essence and function of the Bodhisattva, which constitutes "ability to respond.
The objects of Avalokiteśvara (World-Sound) are sentient beings who, through suffering, constitute the "mechanism" [of response], which is "ability to evoke.

Thus, within these three characters—object, wisdom, and evocation/response—all the explanations regarding the manifestation of myriad phenomena and the sounding of the world's voices are fully accomplished.
The extraordinary chanting and the phonetic explanations for the world have together enabled all who experience them to leave suffering behind and obtain benefit.
Second, the section on the Bodhisattva concludes:
because the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion universally rescues all at once and causes them all to attain liberation, he is called Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara).
It can be seen. Second, this is the general indication below.
This refers to both object and wisdom together, combining the agent and the object in the heading.

The three characters "contemplation" (*guan*) and so forth represent object and wisdom, as well as the agent and the object; the "agent" (*neng*) refers to the capacity to respond, while the "object" (*suo*) refers to that which is responded to.
How could that which is the object of cognition be said again to be capable of illuminating that which is illuminated?
Second, the citation of the sūtra:
as for "sūtra" (經), it is called a sūtra because its meanings and textual patterns are woven together to manifest and develop the mind of the practitioner.

Since this chapter has circulated separately in the world, its titles have mostly been *Guānshìyīn jīng* (The Scripture of Avalokiteśvara) or *Guānshìyīn Púsà Pǔmén pǐn jīng* (The Scripture on the Universal Gate Chapter of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara).
Therefore, following the mention of the person's name, I shall briefly explain the character *jīng* (scripture). Regarding the meaning of "by way of":
the *Jìngmíng xuányì* (Mysterious Meaning of the Vimalakīrti) states that because it proceeds from the minds and mouths of the sages, it is called a *jīng*; it is all-encompassing (*xī*).
The *Dānjiàojiāo* (Teaching of the Dharma Seal) is called a "sūtra" because it proceeds from the mind and mouth of the Tathāgata.
It is also said that from the sages of antiquity to the sages of later times, there are none who have not passed through this teaching of the *Siddhānta* to achieve the Way.

Regarding the phrase "the patterns and principles," this takes the meaning of warp and woof; the dharma and the parable are combined with clarity, and the principle and the pattern mutually manifest one another to weave together the practitioner.
This is the mind of contemplative wisdom.
Second, under the "Universal Gate" (Pumen), the explanation of the dharma encompasses two parts; first, the explanation of the dharma, which begins with the analysis of the two characters.
Regarding "Universal Gate": "Universal" (Pu) has the meaning of pervasiveness, and "Gate" (Men) refers to that which enables passage.
Second, using "one" to illustrate "ten universals":
because the one true reality (shixiang) opens ten universal gates (pumen) without any obstruction, it is called the "Universal Gate.
As for "true reality," the three thousand [realms] are all true reality; when their characteristics are said to be perfectly interfused, "one" signifies the meaning of non-duality.

The myriad virtues are collectively designated as the various names of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The following ten meanings demonstrate its characteristics: first, unconditioned compassion; second, non-conceptual great vows;
third, the practice of perfect cultivation; fourth, cessation that is non-interruption; fifth, the dharma-gate of perfect entry; sixth, indeterminate supernatural powers;
seventh, expedient means within the essence of the body; eighth, the bestowal of the opening of the Dharma; ninth, [the teaching of] preaching; tenth, [the teaching of] liberation.
Universally making offerings to all Buddhas (1), universally benefiting all sentient beings (2), establishing practice from vows (3), the fruit of its own cause (4),

the total manifestation of function (5), making offerings above and benefiting below (6), beginning and end encompassing all phenomena (7), the ten being entirely real (8), mutual interpenetration and universal inclusion without obstruction (9),
and [the tenth]. These ten are all truly real, mutually pervasive, and encompassing without hindrance.
Second, the "Preface to the Chapter.
A "chapter" (*pin*) refers to a category; because items of similar meaning follow one another, it is called a chapter.

Although this title was established according to the separate circulation [of the text], it is nonetheless a single chapter concerning the propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; therefore, it is now prefaced here.

This is to ensure that the fundamental source is not forgotten. The *Madhyama Āgama* states that *varga* is translated here as "chapter" (*pin*), meaning that those passages with similar thematic categories are collected into a single section.
Second, the explanation of the main text of the two great divisions: first, an illustration of the magnitude of the division.

Since this great treatise already contains five chapters that clarify its meaning, the present chapter follows this precedent by providing an explanation through five points: first, the explanation of the title; second, the determination of the essence;
third, the clarification of the primary thesis; fourth, the analysis of the function; and fifth, the delineation of the pedagogical characteristics.
The explanations in the five chapters of the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) are extremely detailed; how could the wondrous meaning of a single chapter of the sutra differ from them?

However, while those chapters primarily clarify the general title consisting of five characters, what we are now explaining is the specific title of this particular chapter. Furthermore, because it concerns the practice of the pit (the *khangxing*), it is necessary to establish five distinct meanings for analysis.
Although these are established independently, they must still accord with that [text] which reveals the Perfect through the opening of the provisional.

Because its phrasing is sublime, explaining its names reveals that both person and dharma are purely sublime; clarifying its essence shows that principle and wisdom are non-dual; elucidating its tenet demonstrates that response and resonance are inconceivable;
discussing its function reveals that bestowing and uprooting are without conditions; and determining its teaching shows it to be the ultimate *amṛta* (clarified butter).
These five chapters comprise three general categories and five specific ones; thus, the teaching is categorized according to the general and the specific (*yǒngbié*). (And so forth.)
Second, the explanation of the title; fifth, the explanation of the present text. First, the explanation of the title has two parts:
first, a general explanation, and second, a specific explanation.
Second, "the general" refers to the indication of characteristics below.
The "comprehensive" [explanation] clarifies both person and dharma together, while the "distinct" [explanation] analyzes person and dharma separately.
Third, as for the section below concerning the faculties (*indriya*):
why is it that, because the conditions have sharp or dull capacities, there are explanations that are extensive or abbreviated?

Since "comprehensive" (*paryāya*) is a brief [teaching], it generally corresponds to those of sharp faculties; since "analytical" (*vibhaṅga*) is an extensive [teaching], it generally corresponds to those of dull faculties. If one must clarify both aspects in a twofold manner:
for the retention of what is heard (*śrutadhara*), the extensive explanation is beneficial for the sharp; for the retention of meaning (*arthadhara*), the brief explanation is beneficial.
One may understand that Paṇḍaka was called "dull" based on his hearing, while Maudgalyāyana was designated as "dull" because— [The text here appears to be truncated.]

This is an explanation based on the general meaning. Regarding the two current interpretations, they correspond to two types of faculties; one must explain them according to their general meaning through a mutual discussion of sharp and dull faculties.
Fourth, we now proceed to the main explanation, which has two parts: first, the general explanation, which begins with the heading and enumeration.
Now, for the general explanation, there are four parts: first, listing the names; second, the sequence; third, the interpretation; and fourth, the analysis.
Second, within the section on listing the names, there is the formal explanation; third, the initial brief indication.
First, regarding the explanation of the names, ten meanings serve as a general interpretation.
Second, regarding the intent behind establishing these names, there are two parts: first, clarifying that the principle transcends names and numbers.
Why is this so? Because the ultimate reality is pure, being nameless and signless, neither a phenomenon (*dharma*) nor a person, and it transcends all measures and quantities.
It is not one, two, or three.

Although the Great Master uses ten thematic gateways to provide a general explanation of the title, he deeply realizes that the Perfect Man Avalokiteśvara and the wondrous Dharma of the Universal Gate are fundamentally beyond verbal expression;
because the characteristics of mental objects are transcended, it is said that "the ultimate principle is pure and serene."
Because they are equal, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All verbal expressions are provisional names without reality; they merely follow deluded thoughts and cannot be found.
Second, from "But the subtle...
onwards, the numerical categories reveal the principle. This section has two parts: first, the demonstration according to the meaning.

However, because the wondrous principle is empty and pervasive, and because names and characteristics are provisionally established within that which is nameless and characteristic-less, we establish names for the nameless and provisionally designate persons and dharmas;
thus, although they do not possess numerical quantity, we nevertheless discuss their quantity.
The previous statement that "the ultimate principle is pure and without names or characteristics" refers to its self-realization being beyond words and thought.

The present statement that "the wondrous principle is empty and pervasive, explained through provisional names and characteristics" is spoken from the perspective of establishing teachings for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the term "empty and pervasive," this clarifies that the wondrous principle lacks any fixed nature; although it has no names or categories, it is nonetheless all-pervasive.
Because it corresponds to all names and numbers, Jingxi said: "The nature is originally nameless, yet it is fully endowed with all names;
therefore, though there is nothing to be said, one speaks, and this speaking constitutes the teaching. Thus, both departing from words and relying on words accord with the ultimate principle;
the Sage’s silence and the Sage’s speech both possess great benefit. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* asks: "If all dharmas are ineffable..."
Question: How can sentient beings, who are by nature inconceivable, accord with this and thereby gain entry? Answer:

If one knows that although all phenomena are spoken of, there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken; and although they are contemplated, there is neither a contemplator nor anything to be contemplated—this is called "accordance.
To be free from such contemplation is called "gaining entry. Now, in this same way, by means of these ten...
The various meanings are unspeakable, yet they are spoken with the intention that students may contemplate without conceptualization.
For this reason, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites scriptural passages as proof, stating:
"Prajñā is a single dharma; the Buddha speaks of it by various names according to the different types of sentient beings."
Regarding the establishment of distinct characters:
the markless Prajñā is itself the single *siddhānta*, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it is established under various names.
Third, "Now, in this section below," correctly lists the names; first, it clarifies the middle [section], which is appropriate.
Now, speaking from a middle standpoint, I shall briefly employ ten points to explain and clarify the intended meaning.
I establish these ten points to avoid being either too extensive or too concise; for excessive extensiveness causes the intellect to recoil, while excessive brevity renders the meaning incomplete.
I now speak from a middle standpoint so that the meaning may be easily understood.
The twenty meanings are formally listed below.

As for the ten meanings: first, person and dharma; second, compassion and wisdom; third, merit and insight; fourth, the true and the responsive; fifth, medicine and the jewel; sixth, the hidden and the manifest;
seventh, the provisional and the real; eighth, the fundamental and the trace; ninth, the conditions and the realization; tenth, wisdom and severance.
Second, regarding the sequence: first, the third section initially indicates two meanings. First, the actual indication; second, the sequence.
This [sequence] has two meanings: first, explaining the sequence in terms of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); second, explaining the sequence in terms of the teaching (*deśanā*).
Regarding both contemplation (*guan*) and teaching (*jiao*), each possesses its own sequential order without confusion.
Second, regarding contemplation, the following clarifies the comprehensive inclusion:

in terms of contemplation, it encompasses the initial, middle, and final stages of mind, wherein the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled; in terms of teaching, it subsumes the gradual, the sudden, and the Small Vehicle.

In the various Mahāyāna sūtras, whether through contemplation or instruction, that which can encompass and include all—contemplating the three minds as a whole, the persons and dharmas, compassion, and the initial mind;
the merit and wisdom of the middle mind; the true and responsive [bodies] up to the eighth; and the ultimate nature of the conditions and causes—is revealed only in the final mind.
When perfect wisdom has severed all afflictions to their ultimate end and the fruit of clarity is finally fulfilled, the teaching—concerning which there are five periods—is fully encompassed.

The *Avataṃsaka* represents the sudden (*tun*), while the other three periods represent the gradual (*jian*). Furthermore, within the gradual, the Tripiṭaka is exclusively Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), while the two "Butter" periods (the *Madhyamāgama* and *Saṃyuktāgama*) are Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it emerges from the preceding four flavors; it is not "mixed" (*miśra*), but rather "counter-balanced" (*pratipakṣa*) and "associated" (*saṃprayukta*). These various explanations have already been prepared.
Therefore, I shall now briefly omit them.

Second, regarding the contemplation of the lower [stages], there are two parts to the explanation of these two meanings: first, the contemplation; second, the sequence. First, regarding persons and dharmas:
first, the nine pairs of subjects that can be encompassed.

Regarding the principle that "person and dharma" are placed first in the contemplation, this is intended to clarify that contemplative practice must necessarily have its practitioner; the practitioner must, in turn, uphold the Dharma.

For example, when a person receives the retribution of a single lifetime, they are formed by grasping the aggregates (*skandhas*). Although such a person may possess immeasurable virtuous conduct, one must first designate their name.
Therefore, placing "person and dharma" at the beginning is based on this same analogy.
Since the nine qualities, beginning with compassion, all take persons and dharmas as their basis, the title of this chapter specifically highlights these two.

Therefore, the analogies of ordinary beings—both provisional and real—are employed first; for only when there is a sentient being formed by the aggregation of the aggregates can one discuss their various virtuous practices.
Is it not thus that persons and dharmas crown these nine meanings?
Regarding the sequence of the two categories of person and phenomenon (pudgala-dharma) as presented below in the formal analysis:
it may be acceptable for person and phenomenon to occupy the beginning of the nine meanings; however, for what reason are they arranged in this specific order?
With what intention is the sequence of "person" and "dharma" established as the vehicle?

Since the dharma is that which is mounted and the person is the mounter, it would be logical to first explain the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) as the vehicle before discussing initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya*) as the mounter; why, then, is this reversed here?
Second, this must be explained below.

This "this" refers to the Sūtra; the Sūtra says, "For this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara. Thus, having first identified the person, it subsequently states, "By the power of skillful means, he manifests through the Universal Gate.
This then discusses the Dharma-person: because the person is able to uphold the Dharma, it is called "person."
This is the Dharma.

Regarding the sequence of the "one who mounts" (the practitioner) and the "that which is mounted" (the Dharma), there are two intended meanings: first, the person comes before the Dharma, as according to the scriptural text;
second, it follows the convenience of the meaning, wherein the person is able to uphold the Dharma—this is precisely that meaning.

Second, regarding compassion: this is because the person who is Avalokiteśvara contemplates the reality-mark (*dharmatā*) and attains the Dharma of the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*). In all subsequent sections below, these two [compassion and wisdom] appear in sequence as a standard pattern.
Second, as for compassion: it arises precisely from the contemplation of the person of Avalokiteśvara upon the Dharma of the Universal Gate.
Since all sentient beings are likewise identical to this principle of the true reality that is neither human nor unrighteous, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. This principle is perfectly complete and lacks nothing.

How is it that while the principle is fully present within sentient beings, their minds are deluded, inverted, and afflicted by suffering? Having contemplated this, one immediately gives rise to compassion and makes a vow.

To extract suffering and bestow happiness is precisely what clarifies compassion (*karuṇā*). Furthermore, if one follows the convenience of verbal expression, placing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) first and compassion last, this is because it accords with the Bodhisattva’s fundamental intention:
first wishing to bestow great happiness through loving-kindness, and since that happiness cannot yet be obtained, subsequently extracting suffering through great compassion.
Thus, loving-kindness comes first and compassion last. If, however, one follows the sequence of their actual application, one first extracts suffering through great compassion.

Subsequently, one bestows happiness through great compassion; furthermore, because practitioners first liberate others from suffering and later cause them to receive happiness, compassion comes first and compassion follows.
The present sequence follows the former meaning.

Next, regarding the discussion of compassion toward sentient beings: once a Great Being has contemplated the universal Dharma of the fundamental nature and realized the principle that there is no difference between living beings and Buddhas, they take pity on those who are deluded and suffering in vain, having lost their original bliss;
thus they give rise to a vow to eternally deliver them. This contemplation of the object and the arousal of the mind properly follow this sequence: first compassion, then [joy].

Regarding the four explanations of the term "compassionate one" (*karuṇika*), I now follow the sequence of the phrasing and my original intention, rather than following the order of application or the practitioner;
thus, the conclusion states: "I now follow the former meaning."
Regarding the three [categories] of merit and wisdom:

as for these three aspects of merit and wisdom, the first—where person and dharma mutually support one another—is based on faith; the second—compassion that both bestows and removes—is what clarifies the aspiration;
to fulfill this aspiration, one must necessarily engage in practice, and such practice does not transcend merit and wisdom. Wisdom... [is the third].
That is to say, the merit of *prajñā* consists of the five perfections (*pāramitā*) mutually supporting and guiding one another to carry out the task of fulfilling vows;
thus, when the principle is perfectly fulfilled, if wisdom increases and clarifies, the vow of great compassion is fulfilled and the meaning of "extracting from suffering" is accomplished.

If merit is profound and vast, the vow of great kindness is fulfilled and the meaning of "bestowing happiness" is accomplished. Therefore, merit and wisdom occupy the [final] three positions. Furthermore, as verbal expression is more convenient, they are presented first.
Regarding merit followed by wisdom: if one intends primarily to transform others through the benefit of actual wisdom, yet they are not yet capable of it, one first demonstrates merit as a support;
thus, merit comes first to provide the resources, and wisdom comes first to provide the guidance.

Regarding the person who relies on the Dharma through faith, their vows precede their practice. Having first contemplated the perfect Dharma, they establish their reliance upon faith and patience, thereby founding the Four Great Vows.
Were it not for the mountain of practice, one could never fill the ocean of vows. Practice is the meaning of merit and wisdom;
it consists of the six perfections, five of which rely upon wisdom. Wisdom guides these five, just as eyes and feet cannot be lacking one another.

The wisdom that eliminates the obstacle of phenomena and the wisdom that dissolves delusions regarding principle—when these two functions are perfected, one awakens to principle and attains phenomena.

Thus we know that merit and wisdom precede, while the functions of compassion and salvation follow. That merit comes first and wisdom second is merely for the sake of linguistic convenience and does not accord with the fundamental intent.
If one discusses their roles as support and guidance, what priority or sequence could there be?
Regarding the four true emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*):
if the wisdom of these four true emanations becomes increasingly luminous, it accords with the *dharmatā*. This *dharmatā* is the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is named the *dharmakāya*.

Once the *dharmakāya* is manifested, one can arise from the True as an emanation; the arising of the emanation occurs precisely because the True is manifested, which is due solely to merit and wisdom.

Because they are developed, they follow in sequence as four. Furthermore, if one considers the skillful means used to transform sentient beings, the provisional (the *ōngyō*) is employed first and the real (the *shinnyo*) is employed later;
following this former sense, they are established in sequence.
Faith, aspiration, merit, and wisdom all reside in the cause; because the cause is able to produce the fruit, they become the Real and the Provisional. Merit serves as the support for...
Wisdom manifests the true body (*dharmakāya*), while wisdom guides merit to manifest its application; thus, the true and the responsive appear in sequence.

Furthermore, if one proceeds according to gradual transformation, first the responsive body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is shown to accommodate those of lesser capacity, and only later are they led into the reality where the true body is revealed.

Alternatively, one might first employ the sudden and then the gradual, in which case the true body precedes and the responsive follows. However, here we do not follow such provisional arrangements of transformation, but rather proceed directly from the perspective of the true manifestation.
It should be established in its proper sequence; thus, it is said "from the preceding" for the sake of linguistic convenience.
Regarding the "five medicinal jewels":
first, the two bodies—the *dharmakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*—are explained directly as the realization attained [by the Buddha], which has not yet involved benefiting others. Now...
It clarifies that both bodies are capable of benefiting sentient beings: the True Body (dharmakāya) eliminates grasping at signs, analogous to medicine;
the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya) accords with myriad capacities, analogous to a pearl. To clarify the sequence by means of these two characters, they correspond to compassion and wisdom.
Because the two practices of merit and wisdom manifest the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), they are called "direct speech.

Since this refers to the realization [attained by those] who have not yet engaged with those of sharp faculties, it now clarifies the medicinal pearl to demonstrate how the two bodies benefit sentient beings. When the True Body accords with the profound principle, seeing it causes the three delusions to be entirely eliminated;
this is the benefit of curing illnesses. When the Responsive Body accords with the responses of sentient beings, all manner of virtues gather universally; this is like the falling rain.

"Treasure" means benefit. It is said that for one who truly destroys the grasping at marks, since the three wisdoms (trividya) take the profound principle as their reality, how could they merely destroy the grasping at views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa)?

One should know that views and afflictions grasp the marks of birth-and-death (saṃsāra), the [countless] sands of phenomena grasp the mark of nirvāṇa, and ignorance grasps the marks of the two extremes.
Whether gradual or non-gradual, both meanings are present; this is like the sequence of medicinal herbs and pearls.

Regarding the similarity between [the two methods] and compassion: the medicine is analogous to compassion, while the pearl is comparable to loving-kindness (*maitrī*). These four meanings establish their sequence.

In terms of the original intent of the teaching, loving-kindness comes first and compassion follows; however, in terms of function and according to the capacity of the practitioner, one first removes suffering and subsequently bestows benefit.
The present order appears to correspond to the latter two of these.
Regarding the "sixfold manifestation of the hidden":
as for the sixfold manifestation of the luminous and the hidden, the previous explanation of the principle of the two bodies was able to manifest the benefit;

now, in distinguishing how they accord with conditions to obtain either hidden benefit or manifest benefit, the [explanation] follows after the two bodies. Thus, the latter part is explained after the two bodies.

The preceding section clarified that the two bodies dispel delusions, like medicine applied to a specific ailment, or like a jewel responding to its conditions. Since delusions have been dispelled, the true body is revealed;
therefore, it is said that the two bodies are "manifest benefits" (*khyāna-anugraha*). Now, we shall distinguish how these two bodies constantly and universally benefit sentient beings:
those who see and know them are called "manifest benefits," while those who do not see or know them are termed "latent benefits" (*tirobhūta-anugraha*). Thus it is said.
This concludes the section on the Sage’s manifestations that benefit sentient beings. As for the sequence of these two types of benefit, it cannot be definitively determined;
they are described as "mysterious" and "manifest" merely according to the convenience of the discourse. Since this point is easily understood, it is not further elaborated upon here.
Regarding the seventh section on the provisional and the real:

as for the clarification of the provisional and the real, the reason why the benefits derived from the preceding conditions differ in their underlying intent is precisely because the power of the two wisdoms—provisional skillfulness being manifold and responding to capacities with perfect appropriateness, never missing what is fitting—is such that this [section] follows next; first the provisional, then...

The "real" (śūnyatā/paramārtha) is ranked according to depth; if one follows the literal text, the real benefit comes first and the provisional measure second—this is a sequence established according to the capacities of beings.

However, regarding the Buddha’s original intent, he first acted solely for the sake of the single great cause and condition (ekamahākaruṇāhetu-pratyaya), first manifesting the real benefit for sentient beings who were not yet capable, and only later employing the provisional measure.
That the prior conditions differ refers to the distinctions in the capacities and natures of those being reached;
that expedient skillfulness is "without fixed direction" means that the wisdom capable of discerning them has no settled location.

Whether acting in obscurity or manifestation, whether destroying evil or generating good, the differences in depth and breadth all arise from the non-discrepant meeting of these two types of wisdom; thus, in terms of benefit—

Regarding the subsequent discussion on the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, although there are three meanings concerning their sequence, they are arranged here according to their relative depth.

Within the eight sections on the "Original and the Traced," although the skillful means of the provisional and the real benefit sentient beings, such skillful means possess degrees of excellence and inferiority; it must necessarily be...

The distinctions between superior, middling, and inferior wisdom, as well as between the fundamental and the manifested (*honji-suijaku*), and between the provisional and the real, are here treated both briefly and horizontally.
Now, I wish to precisely judge their relative heights and depths to clarify the stages of progression.

Since the manifestations of the provisional and the real are wondrous because their fundamental source is high, I shall therefore, following the general summary, explain the capacity for these subtle and wondrous workings. For there can be no manifestation without the wood; thus, I first clarify the wood.
Without the provisional traces (*jì*), the fundamental reality (*běn*) cannot be manifested; therefore, the traces should come first.
When it is said that there is a gradation of skill, this refers to the superiority or inferiority of wisdom. Regarding the categories of superior, middling, and inferior:

the Subtle Enlightenment (*miàojiào*) constitutes the superior, the Perfect Enlightenment (*shàngjiào*) constitutes the middling, and those descending from these constitute the inferior. Since the prior application of the provisional and the real must reflect the capacities of sentient beings, both must necessarily be employed together.

"Horizontal" refers to the clouds; "vertical" refers to the fact that since this current teaching discusses the relative heights of the original and the manifested in terms of their stages, one must first follow the original before the manifested can descend—hence it is called "vertical.
Thus, the sequence of these two dharmas can be clearly seen.

The ninth section concerns the "condition as the cause of clear comprehension" (*pariccheda-hetu-pratyaya*). First, it refers back to the preceding [sections] which accord with the treatise regarding self and others.
Regarding the "cause as the condition for clear comprehension": above, the practitioner has generated the resolve and engaged in cultivation;

from cause to fruition, their transformation of others and benefitting of beings vary in depth. From the person and the Dharma up to the True and the Responsive [Bodies], this is the sequence of one's own practice, like medicine or a jewel.

The sequence from "original" (*ben*) to "traces" (*ji*) concerns the stages of transforming others; this follows the order of the discourse but does not yet constitute a tracing back to the fundamental root.
As for the eight pairs mentioned above, which proceed from the subtle to the manifest, these likewise follow the order of the discourse and have not yet been analytically assigned.
Now, in drawing from the current flow to seek its source, one must clarify the inherent virtues (*xingde*) as the basis from which all phenomena arise.
Second, to now further examine the seeds:
if we trace back the nature-virtue seeds, for those who possess contemplative wisdom, the compassionate mind, vows, and the adornment of wisdom manifest the True Body;
these are all the seeds of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (causes of penetration). If it is the Dharma of the Universal Gate, the compassionate mind and vows...
The manifestation of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) through the adornment of merit and virtue occurs because all such manifestations take conditional causes as their seeds;
this constitutes the ninth stage.

By tracing back from this, one realizes that the person who possesses the wisdom, compassion, vows, and contemplative insight of the true body (dharmakāya) originally relies upon the "revealing cause" (vijñapti-hetu) of inherent virtue.

Regarding the seeds: if one considers the merit of the *saṃbhogakāya* and the Dharma-gate of universal vows, these originate fundamentally from the nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) as the causal condition for seeds.

Since this is the case for one’s own practice, it serves as an analogy for transforming others. When fundamental realization is attained, the wisdom of ultimate benefit belongs to the "revealed seed" (*miao zhong*), while the medicinal king (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) pertains to the "understanding seed.

When manifesting through provisional transformation, the wisdom of expedient benefit belongs to the "traced seed" (*ji zhong*), and the pearl king (*Maṇirāja*) attributes its merit to the "conditioned seed. This is explained according to the sequential order.
Next, regarding the tenfold investigation of the conditions, causes, and fruits of knowledge and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*): the previous section clarified the conditions, causes, and fruits;
this section clarifies knowledge and abandonment. The former was an investigation into the source of the causes, while the present is a sequential clarification of knowledge and abandonment.
Regarding the ultimate beginning: it originates from the *vidyā-hetu* (cause of enlightenment) and culminates in the great wisdom of *bodhi*;

it originates from the *pratyaya-hetu* (causal condition) and culminates in the merit of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*) that is *nirvāṇa*. Because all conditioned activities cease upon entering *nirvāṇa*, it is placed in the tenth stage.
Having previously traced back in reverse to the beginning of the causal virtues, we now proceed in forward order to the end of the resultant virtues;
thus, based on this sequence from beginning to end, the second section follows. Since the character "過" (guò) lacks the radical "荼" (tú), the ten [stages] are not discussed thereafter.
Second, regarding the subsequent clarification of the stages of the teaching, there are two parts: first, citing the chapter headings to establish the gates.
Second, regarding the clarification of the sequence according to the various teachings, there are both general and specific aspects.
Regarding the second [the general], the general meaning is easy to understand. As for the two general meanings explained below according to the gates, first, as for the "general":
the general meaning is intelligible.

The ten [categories] may be discussed for each of the five periods and four teachings according to their respective doctrines; however, they cannot be exhaustively investigated. For instance, regarding the establishment of the ten pairs in the Tripiṭaka:

"person and dharma" refers to the fact that persons are formed by grasping the aggregates (*skandha*), while dharmas consist of the truths (*satya*) and the means of deliverance (*nairyāṇika-dharma*);

"compassion" refers to the *śrāvaka*s taking sounds as their object and the *bodhisattva*s taking living beings as their object; and "merit and wisdom" refers to the three trainings (*śikṣā*) of the *śrāvaka*s and the six perfections (*pāramitā*) of the *bodhisattva*s.

Regarding the True and the Responsive: the fivefold Dharma-body constitutes the "intentional" (saṃdhāya), while the medicinal pearl constitutes the "responsive" (pratyupasthita) that cures the diseases of the four abidings.
Regarding the rain of the Three Vehicles' jewels: the "hidden and manifest" refers to sentient beings obtaining benefit whether they see and hear [the teaching] or do not see and hear it.

Regarding the provisional and the real: the "real" accords with the truth, while the "provisional" follows worldly sentiment. Regarding the fundamental and the trace: the "fundamental" is what one realizes for oneself, while the "trace" is what is manifested for others.
Regarding "conditioning and completing": a single phrase contains the seeds of the subtle goodness of the completing cause and the wisdom of conditions; regarding "severance":
the four fruits of the śrāvaka and the sudden realization of the bodhisattva are established, such that the three baskets are fully prepared, and both the general and specific meanings can be known.

Second, the specific explanation of the present [teaching] below is divided into two parts: first, the five flavors; second, the initial explanation of the five [flavors]. First, regarding milk: it clarifies that it possesses the previous six meanings.
Specifically, the present teaching shall now be explained: as for the name of the *Avataṃsaka* Sudden Teaching, it is the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*; according to its title, first...
When a person of enlightenment upholds the Dharma, they must necessarily possess compassion; as a Bodhisattva cultivating the causes, they naturally possess both merit and wisdom.

Having entered the stages (*bhūmi*), they will surely realize the True and the Responsive. Being able to benefit sentient beings, they can distinguish between medicinal herbs and pearls, so that those who receive their aid obtain benefit—both through the hidden and the manifest.

Because the milk is immediately [contained within] the curd, the six-character specific title of the *Avataṃsaka*—which fully possesses both the Dharma and the metaphor—is "Mahāvaipulya-dharma" (The Great and Vast Dharma).
"Buddha" refers to the person who is the fruition of Śākyamuni. "Avataṃsaka" is a metaphor for the causal flowers of the various stages (*bhūmi*) and the resultant virtues of the fruition.
Even considering this single title alone, it already contains these six meanings; for from compassion up to the true and the responsive, they do not transcend that which arises from itself.

The practice of cause and effect, the medicinal pearl, and the manifestation of darkness are merely the transformation of others; the subject and object therein are discussed separately as six meanings within the Middle Way.

Second, from "while yet" onwards, it clarifies the absence of the latter four meanings. This section has two parts: first, it clarifies the general and the specific; first, it clarifies that there is no distinction.

However, regarding those who have not yet attained the distinct discourse on the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the trace, or the conditions and the fulfillment, as well as wisdom and cessation:
while the meaning of "pervasion" (tong) is permitted in the lower [teachings],
there is pervasion in terms of meaning but none in terms of distinctness.

If one discusses the provisional and the real, as well as the substantial function, in terms of the primary and secondary, the subtle cause, and the conditions for the wisdom and abandonment of Great Enlightenment, there is likewise a principle to be found therein.
Second, regarding the section "Why [is it so]? below, this clarifies the deficiency and the completeness; first, it clarifies the deficiency with respect to the beginning of the transformation.

Why is this so? Because the Buddha’s single-period of teaching to transform sentient beings clarifies both the sudden and the gradual; although the sudden teaching is expounded, the gradual teaching has not yet been fully revealed, and thus the four intentions are not clarified therein.

The four explanations—of the provisional and the real, and so forth—demonstrate the intent for appearing in the world, showing that what was accomplished long ago is now being brought back, and that the three causes ultimately converge in the secret treasury.

Regarding the first point, when the Tibetan [tradition] was initially established, the teaching was specifically designed to accommodate those of great capacity; since it was not intended as a final consummation, it lacks this particular intent.

Regarding the second point, the following section clarifies the presence and absence of these two [aspects] by contrasting them with the *Lotus Sūtra*. First, the contrast with the *Lotus Sūtra*: [text follows].
The reason it is not clear is that in those sutras, the Small Vehicle is shown to be separated from the Great Vehicle, like one who is deaf or mute;

this provisional means covers [the truth] so that its reality is not yet revealed. Therefore, it is said, "I have long kept silent on this matter and have not hurried to speak of it," which implies there is no distinction between the provisional and the real.
