which is translated here as "Right and Universal Knowledge. Since the single true mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*) opens ten gates, these three meanings, if explained in detail,
could not be exhausted even in a lifetime lasting for many kalpas.
The third chapter, "On the Attainment of Peace," establishes ten meanings through scriptural evidence.
I have personally searched the "Universal Gate" (Pumen) chapter for the meaning of the ten universals to corroborate this.

For instance, when Avalokiteśvara takes pity upon the fourfold assembly and accepts their necklaces, "various" (zhū) refers to names that are not one, and "pity" (mǐn) carries the meaning of compassion. This...
That is to say, universal compassion is the spontaneous presence of great vows; this is the universal meaning.
To travel through various lands in manifold forms to deliver sentient beings is precisely what it means to purify Buddha-fields. Is this not the practice of universality?

"Liberation" is a term that signifies universality. Is it not the case that the universal manifestation of the gates of severing delusions is the universal entry into the Dharma-gates?
The universal power of skillful means is the universal power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).
To preach the Dharma universally is to preach the Dharma universally; to bring great benefit is to universally mature sentient beings. [This is] divided as follows:

"Offering two parts to the two Tathāgatas is equivalent to making offerings to all Buddhas. This meaning and intent apply universally; since it is fully present within the scriptural text, I cite it here as proof.

The second major section, "Explaining the Essence," has two parts: first, a brief indication of the essence of this chapter; second, the specific demonstration of its current essence. First, the demonstration of the current essence.
The second explanation regarding the essence [of the Buddha-nature] is that its essence consists of the union of numinous wisdom with the Dharma-body.

"Numinous wisdom" refers to initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*), while the "Dharma-body" refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Since they are one and the same awakening, what need is there to speak of their "union"?

It is merely because of fundamental delusion that awakening becomes non-awakening. Through the stages of the path of cultivation, one seeks the name; through the name, one awakens to the source. This merit is not [attained by] effort.

The meaning of "conformity" (*he*) through subduing and severing has not yet been fully established; while the five grades [of the Path of Training] are termed "sudden subduing," they are called "conformity" (*guan-he*) when the six sense organs appear to conform, and "partial true conformity" (*fen-zhen zheng-he*) when it is realized.
Now, the "conformity" (*he*) of Avalokiteśvara that borders upon the ultimate is fundamentally the beginning of the original [enlightenment].

It is not two distinct entities, for because there is non-awakening (*abodha*), one speaks of "conformity" in terms of subduing and severing; the original awakening (*benjue*) serves as the guiding principle and sustenance for the arising of initial awakening (*shijue*).
Because it is understood, it is called "Dharma" (the Teaching). Because it naturally gathers three thousand sublime virtues, it is called "Body.

Because its original awakening is primordially luminous, it is called "Numen" (Spirit). Because it can now sever [delusions] and realize [truth], it is called "Wisdom. The non-duality of the fundamental and the initial is the essence that is elucidated.
Second, regarding the other [scriptures] that differ from this sutra: first, they are distinguished by means of three and two.
If other sutras clarify the three bodies, they do so by taking the dharma-body alone as the essence;
since this chapter contains only the meaning of two bodies, it takes the union of principle and wisdom as the essence.

Regarding the elucidation of the three bodies (*trikāya*) in other sutras, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* establishes the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). It further states:

and the nature of phenomena is the dharma [body]. This sutra’s *Jiemo* (Trace Gate) section states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the reality of all phenomena."

If the five Buddhas of the marks were able to exhaustively investigate this retribution, its true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and its fundamental dharma-gate, it would be as stated in the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*:
"The Tathāgata knows and sees the marks of the triple world as they truly are—neither identical nor different.

In that case, the Tathāgata would have known and seen this retribution as neither identical nor different. Furthermore, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, there is a liberation called "inconceivable" (*acintya*). [This would be that very liberation.]
The abiding of the Dharma is liberation; this is the retribution [of practice], which is able to place Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed.

This corresponds to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the three types of *Prajñāpāramitā*, as well as the three bodies (*trikāya*). In these various sūtras, all may be correlated with the essence, substance, and function of the three bodies.

As for this chapter, where there is only the meaning of two bodies: the one named Avalokiteśvara represents the meaning of the True Body (*dharmakāya*), while the "Universal Gate" (*samantamukha*) demonstrates [the other].

The "Manifest" (pratyutpanna) refers to the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body); "True" (*satya*) is the wisdom of internal realization, while "Response" (*pratibhāsa*) is the body for external transformation.

When compared with various sūtras, this constitutes the primary application of our school. Although there is no explicit textual passage regarding its substance, the meaning of its substance is present;

for since wisdom does not exist in isolation, it must be conjoined with the *dharmakāya*. How could there be a lid without a chest, or light without a mirror? Thus, these are the three bodies (*trikāya*) according to the various sūtras.

Therefore, it can be distinguished that the *dharmakāya* serves as the essence for this [first] body, whereas for these two bodies [of the second category], the *dharma* and *saṃbhoga* must be combined to constitute the essence.
Second, from "only this" onwards, it clarifies the non-duality of wisdom and principle; first, it explains this non-duality by way of their emergence from entanglement.
This very wisdom is itself the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Why is this? If there were no numinous wisdom, the true mark would remain hidden and is termed the *tathāgatagarbha*.

As stated previously, when numinous wisdom accords with the *dharmakāya*, it is not a case of two distinct things joining; rather, the very substance of this numinous wisdom is the *dharmakāya* itself.
Because the body consists of fundamental awakening (mūla-avabodha) and non-awakening (an-avabodha), it is called the Tathāgatagarbha while remaining within the bonds of affliction;

because fundamental awakening is self-awakened (sva-avabodha), it is called the Great Dharmakāya when emerging from those bonds. Now that one has emerged from the bonds, the verification of wisdom is itself the principle.
Second, "Now knowing" and below uses the analogy of a single object to illustrate non-duality.

Now, knowing that the provisional and the real are non-dual with principle—just as the names "left" and "right" [refer to the same hand]—is because the characteristics of the provisional and the real are inherently present within the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*);
it is not the case that those of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) possess these qualities of the fundamental nature. Therefore, [it is not so].
Knowing that the provisional and the real share the same essence, one now possesses spiritual wisdom;

having realized that the provisional and the real are non-dual, one understands that although "wisdom of principle" and "wisdom of phenomena" are two names, they refer to but a single essence. It is like a single object: if a person stands to its right, the object becomes its left side;
if the person stands to its left, the object becomes its right side. Although the names "left" and "right" differ, the object itself has never been distinct. Thus, the two wisdoms are one.
The principle and its name are different, yet their substance is one.
Second, regarding the explanation of the extensive reference to the *Daben* (Great Text):
if one clarifies the meaning of the substance of the true mark (*dharmatā*), it is extensively set forth in the *Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning) of the *Daben*.
The third section, "Clarifying the Thesis," establishes that the thesis is "resonance and response" (*ganying*).

Clarifying the thesis: taking resonance and response as the thesis. When the capacities of the ten realms strike it, the tranquility within illumination is revealed, whereby they receive the manifested image.

This reveals that the manifestation [of wisdom] and all joys, as well as quiescence and illumination, are non-dual; they are simply one single cognition. Although "bestowing" and "extracting" differ, how could there be a need for mental movement such that there would be a sequence of before and after?
This refers to the two questions and answers which speak of a sequence, not the time when benefit is actually conferred.
In the second section, "The Benefit of the Text," the essential meaning of the school's tenet is revealed.

Although the text is extensive, it directly subsumes all under the principle of "response and resonance" (ganying), just as pulling a single main rope causes the entire net to move; therefore, response and resonance are established as the central tenet.
The seven calamities, the three poisons, and the two types of seeking—liberation from these; the thirty-three bodies and the nineteen sermons through which beings attained deliverance:
the meaning of these passages is like the meshes of a net. If one pulls the main cord of "resonant response," there is no mesh that does not move.
This is the essential core of the doctrine; who would say otherwise?

this primary section clarifies the cause and effect of the One Vehicle;

From the ordinary person to the sage, there exists the capacity to evoke and that which is evoked; this principle is broad and pervasive, yet not specific to our current thesis.
That the intent of the sutra does not extend to this point reveals the reason why cause and effect are not employed here—namely, because of the wording of the scripture itself.
This is because it does not discuss the personal cultivation and realization of Avalokiteśvara;

How could there be any sign of attaining contemplation or entering a stage? If the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says, "In the past, Avalokiteśvara Buddha taught me... [it refers to a different context].
Entering samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation: first, within the process of hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object;

once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise. Thus gradually increasing, the hearing and that which is heard both come to an end. When the hearing has ended, one does not dwell [in that state];

when the awareness and that which is aware are both empty, the awareness of emptiness becomes perfectly complete, and that which is emptied by emptiness itself ceases. When arising and ceasing have both ceased, there is stillness.
When cessation manifests, one suddenly transcends both the mundane and supramundane worlds, attaining perfect clarity throughout the ten directions and obtaining two extraordinary excellences:
first, above, one accords with the fundamental wondrous enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as all Tathāgatas;
second, below, one accords with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same [nature] as all living beings.
Because they share in the power of compassion through their yearning and reverence, they are able to manifest response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*);
because they share in that yearning and reverence, they are able to bestow fearlessness. Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-citta-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
"In the past, the Tathāgata Śāntasthita-sahasraraśmi-king taught this Greatly Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Mahākaruṇā-citta-dhāraṇī to me with his golden hand."
He placed his hand upon the crown of my head and spoke these words: "You must uphold this heart-mantra and universally bring great benefit to all sentient beings in the degenerate age.
At that time, having first established myself in the First Bhūmi, by hearing this mantra once, I transcended to the Eighth Bhūmi;
furthermore, my body manifested a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, and so forth, as described in the extensive versions of the scripture.

The two preceding chapters extensively clarify the Tathāgata’s cultivation of the causes and realization of the fruit, and such texts concerning the Buddha’s cause and fruit can be found throughout various sūtras;

provides the cause. The phrase "avoiding the seven kinds of difficulties and departing from the roots of the three poisons" provides the fruit.

This is a passage concerning the fruit. As for this passage on cause and fruit, what could possibly be omitted when it encompasses both the past and the future?

Since there is indeed a basis for this within the text itself, the present claim that the text does not reach this point should be understood as follows:
our school does not accept [the notion of] cause and effect, specifically employing "response and stimulus" (ganying). Briefly, there are three reasons for this.

because this wisdom is darkly merged with the principle and belongs to that essence, it takes the inclusion of all phenomena as its thesis. Third, from beginning to end, this single fascicle exclusively elucidates the implicit and the explicit.
The two [sections] on responding to the hidden and manifest capacities—if one applies the essential principles of resonance and response (*ganying*), they will be well established.

Answer 2: Yes.
Answer: It is so.
"So" means that this [response] is also granted as an occasion for the Sage’s mind to illuminate perfectly, leaving nothing of good or evil behind.

Section Two: The Meaning of the Latent Submergence of the Two Natures and the Arising of Clarity.
Part One: The Question. Question: Is the spiritual capacity (indriya) inherently good or not? If it is already good, why is it necessary to elicit the Noble Ones?

Because they do not know that the nature of goodness possesses the capacity for manifestation, this question arises.
There are two answers.
The first answer states: the nature of goodness lies latent and dormant like a lotus in the mud; when a sage responds to conditions, it emerges like the sun shining upon it.
Because it lies hidden in obscurity and has not yet manifested, it must await the response of a Sage; because it is of a virtuous nature, it is able to be brought forth.
Second, regarding the meaning of the mutual relationship between the three—goodness, evil, and compassion—first, the question:
Furthermore, if one says that the "trigger" (*ki*) is the "gate" (*kan*), is it a gate of goodness or a gate of non-goodness? If it is already good, why is there a need for [the Sage]?
If one becomes a Saint of the Passes through goodness, if it were not for this goodness, how could one become a Saint of the Passes? If one becomes non-good, how could one ever become a Saint?
The categories of ordinary and sage are distinct; how have they ever been related?

If goodness has already been perfected, there is no need to rely on the Saints of the Passes; if one relies on the Saints of the Passes, it implies that goodness is still slight and evil is becoming manifest. To rely on the Saints of the Passes [in such a case] is to be preoccupied with evil.
It should also be said that what is slight becomes manifest through evil.
Second, the response:
because the good relates to great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and the evil relates to great pity (*mahākaruṇā*), they are said to be related.
How could the Sage bring about the evils of sentient beings? It is simply that, by the very nature of things, his goodness naturally engages with them through the response of compassion;

thus, when responding to goodness, they achieve goodness and obtain happiness, and when responding to evil, their evil is extinguished and they are freed from suffering. Because he shares the same essence [with them], his engagement is not something separate or external.

The *dharmakāya* gathers immeasurable dharma-gates and is able to correspond to the various modes of contemplative wisdom of sentient beings; the *saṃbhogakāya* gathers... [the fruits of merit].
The third section, consisting of three pairs of contrasts, distinguishes the three [aspects];
first, it clarifies that the response to stimuli is neither identical to nor different from [the stimulus]. First, the question:
He asked again: "Are the stimulus and the response identical or distinct? If they are identical, then the stimulus is itself the response, and the ordinary person would be the sage.
If they are distinct, then they are unrelated.
He gave two answers.
Answer: Response and transformation (ganying) are discussed in terms of being neither identical nor different.
Because they are not identical, there is response; because they are not different, there is mutual connection.
Second, it clarifies that response and transformation are neither unreal nor real. First, the question:

Question: Is this resonance between stimulus and response (ganying) empty or real? If it is real, then ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are real; being real, how can they be transformed? If you say it is empty, what is there to be transformed in emptiness? Second answer: The answer is that resonance is neither exclusively empty nor exclusively real. It is empty because its nature is devoid of self (anātman); it is real because its function of responding to conditions is not non-existent. Because it is empty, there is no fixed substance to be transformed; because it is real, there is the capacity for transformation. Therefore, although the nature of ordinary beings is empty, their deluded habits are substantial; by means of the reality of the Buddha’s power, the emptiness of their nature is revealed, and thus they are transformed. This is why it is said that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) can transform the conditioned (saṃskṛta), and the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) can transform conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya). Thus, resonance is both empty and real. Furthermore, because the principle of resonance is profound and subtle, it is called "empty"; because its responsive function is manifest and efficacious, it is called "real. It is like the moon reflected in water: the moon is empty yet its reflection is real; the water is real yet its essence is empty. Resonance is likewise so. Therefore, one cannot categorically say it is either empty or real. This is the meaning of the second answer.
The answer is as follows.
Regarding the phrase "as stated above" (*yúnyún*): the meaning should be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Since it is neither identical nor different, and neither empty nor real, one must grasp the underlying principle that this state of being both neither empty nor real and neither identical nor different is fundamentally the non-differentiation of the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.

Regarding the non-differentiation of differences: while the three thousand [realms] are identical in principle as they approximate the functional utility of phenomena, they are not one because delusion and enlightenment differ in their phenomenal reality;
yet they are not many because the Buddha-dharma arises in response to awakening, while the mind arises as a response to delusion. Since the fundamental principle is originally one, it is not real;

since phenomena temporarily appear as different, it is not empty. Thus, the *Fahua Wenju* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "The illusory stimulus, the illusory response, the illusory resonance, and the illusory arrival."
Therefore, although the distinct characteristics prior to abiding in the ground still persist, in the true stage each and every part is identical to the Buddha’s essence and function;
when ultimate realization is reached, response and stimulus have ceased, so how can one further discuss oneness or difference, or the empty or the real?
Third, the section "By Others Below" clarifies that the response of resonance is inconceivable. Part two: First, it presents the questions and answers of others.

First, it raises the doubt that the separation between ordinary beings and sages prevents resonance, because [others] ask: the sage is the object of resonance (*pratibhāsa*) while the ordinary being is the agent of resonance; the sage is the one who responds (*pratyudgama*), while the ordinary being... [is the one who initiates].

That which is the object of response is not the agent of response, and that which is the agent of response is not the object of response; how then can one speak of the "path of mutual resonance between stimulus and response"?

To analyze the essence of stimulus and response, their natures are distinct. Although they are established reciprocally as subject (agent) and object (recipient), the categories of ordinary person and sage are fixed:
what is experienced by the sage is necessarily not the stimulus, and what is responded to by the ordinary person is certainly not the response. Thus, stimulus and response are separated.
What is meant by "the intersection of the Way" (*dao-jiao*)?

The second [part] answers that it is so called because of the existence and disappearance of subject and object; thus, there is the "intersection of the Way. First, regarding the mutual discussion of subject and object:

the answer is that what is elicited is in reality without an elicitor; it is from the elicitation that it is named "elicited. It is said that the Sage is the elicited, and that which is to be responded to is the reality.
There is no "responding" that can be designated by the name "that which is to be responded to. Are ordinary beings that which is to be responded to? Or are they the "response" itself?
Is it the capacity to respond or the capacity to be responded to? Is it the response that is the object of the response, or the response that is the subject of the response?
Since there is neither the reality of responding nor the distinction between responding and being responded to, [neither exists].

First, one establishes that the object experienced (*anubhūta*) and the object to be experienced (*anubhavya*) are unreal. Why? Because the object experienced is unreal since it is not supramundane (*alokottara*), and the object to be experienced is unreal since it is not noble (*ārya*).
Next, one establishes that the subject experiencing (*anubhavitr*) and the subject to be experienced (*anubhāvya*) are unreal.

Why? Because one takes that which was previously the object experienced as the subject experiencing; since the object experienced is already unreal, the subject experiencing is unreal. Furthermore, one takes that which was previously the object to be experienced...
Since that which is to be produced by the cause is not real, the cause itself is not real; since both are not real, the two are also not different.
Regarding these two being non-different, each shall be discussed below in terms of its persistence or disappearance.

That which is non-different yet appears different is such that, when the Sage has passed away, what he has manifested is designated as the "responsive" (the object), while for the ordinary person who has passed away, their own response is taken as the "stimulating" (the subject).
Therefore, it is said that the Way of Stimulus and Response intersects.
Since there is neither reality nor difference, how can one speak of the intersection of stimulus and response? Thus, this is established through mutual existence and mutual disappearance.

They are not different yet appear as different because that which is moved constitutes the "responsive" (nengying) and that which is responded to constitutes the "moving" (nenggong); thus, the moving and the responding are not different.

However, in the present, the side of the Sage is submerged within that which is moved and is designated as the "responsive," while the side of the ordinary person is submerged within that which is responded to and is designated as the "moving";
thus, they become different. Because they are different, there exists the relationship of moving and responding.

Because they are not different, one attains the "intercourse of the Way" (*dao-jiao*). This concerns the ancient masters' interpretation of the principles of resonance-response (*gan-ying*) and the intercourse of the Way.

Regarding the two private difficulties [raised by] Xi [Zhi], in the lower chapter Zhǎngān refutes and establishes [the correct view]. First, he refutes that the other's position is untenable; first, within the first part, he refutes that the established thesis is untenable;
first, he clarifies that the concepts of existence and extinction are untenable.

I object to these words: if there were truly no difference between "stimulus" (gan) and "response" (ying), then why is it that when a Sage passes away he can stimulate [the response], whereas an ordinary person passing away can only respond? If this were so, there would be no distinction between the ordinary and the sage.
If this were not so, then stimulus and response would indeed differ; how then can you say they do not differ?

Although one may discuss existence and disappearance through the mutual relationship of the capable [the saint] and the object [the ordinary person], when investigating their essential nature, it is simply that the delusions of the ordinary person disappear from the side of the saint, and the response of the saint disappears from the side of the ordinary person.
Consequently, the saint’s disappearance of the capable should not mean that the ordinary person’s disappearance of the capable can no longer produce a response;
if this were the case, the capacity to respond and the stimulus would be eternally distinct—how then can you say they are not different?
Secondly, regarding the response from below, it clarifies that there is no difference; the general meaning is the same as before.

Furthermore, if the capacity to respond has no reality apart from the capacity to evoke, why is it not called the "capacity to evoke"? If the capacity to respond lacks reality, why is it not called the "object of evocation"?
If this were the case, then there would be no such thing as the interaction between ordinary beings and sages through evocation and response; if it were otherwise, then...
How are these two different, and how are they not different?
Furthermore, the second [section] refutes [the opponent] below by concluding with the fallacies of the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*).

Moreover, it refutes: "If that which is capable of producing is the response to that which is produced, and that which is performed is the capacity for what is to be performed, this is the meaning of self-arising. If...
If "the capable" (the agent) is merely that which is capable, and "the felt" (the object) is merely that which is felt, this would still be the meaning of self-arising.

If the capable were to produce the felt, and the capable produced what is capable of being felt, while the felt produced what is felt, and the felt produced the capable, and the capable produced what is capable of being felt—such that all that is capable of being felt and all that is capable of being felt by the capable are produced from others—is this not the meaning of other-nature? If they were co-arisen...
If [the capacity] were produced, there would be two faults; if it were devoid of these two, it would fall into the fault of being causeless.
This is because that which is felt (the object) belongs to the stimulus (the capacity), and that which is capable of responding (the subject) belongs to the response (the result);

thus, they belong to their own respective natures. Next, although the following two phrases involve the meaning of stimulus and response, they do not depend upon one another and still belong to their own respective natures. Following this, there is...

Since all four positions arise from those [conditions], they belong to the nature of other-dependence (*parabhāva*). The third position—that it arises neither solely from itself nor solely from others, but requires the union of both—is attributed to the nature of commonality (*sādhāraṇabhāva*).
If it were divorced from both self and other, it would belong to the nature of causelessness (*ahetubhāva*).

Second, the question: "If [it is as you say], then there is no response. This section clarifies that the present [teaching] can perfectly accord with reality; it consists of two parts: first, the question regarding the absence of response by way of departing from the four propositions;

second, the answer which employs the four *siddhāntas* to establish causes and conditions. First, the question: "If this is so, then there is no response. Second, the answer: "The Sage... and so forth, responding by establishing causes and conditions through the four *siddhāntas*.
Answer: The Sage employs the dharma of equality and non-abiding; he does not abide in any fixed response, but rather accords with conditions through the four *siddhāntas*.
Because the Great Sage has perfectly realized that the three thousand realms of phenomena and principle are co-present within a single mind, his mind is equal;

because he realizes that each and every thing is empty, provisional, and the Middle, his mind is non-abiding. Since the Sage takes this equality and non-abiding as his capacity [to respond], [he manifests accordingly].
Because it accords with the Dharma, it does not abide in or cling to the specific capacities and stimuli of beings;

rather, it spontaneously responds to the four types of faculties—those who delight in the ten realms, those who seek what is expedient, those who destroy evil, and those who enter into principle—as each faculty strikes upon it.

Through these four kinds of dharmas—the mundane, the personal, the remedial, and the ultimate—it responds naturally and effortlessly. How could this resonance be characterized by self, other, both together, or neither?

Furthermore, regarding the inconceivable nature of this, if sentient beings experience four benefits through their own arising resonance, it may be said that they resonate with and respond to themselves.
If they experience four benefits through three types [of conditions], it may be said that response arises from resonance and resonance arises from response;
together they can produce resonance and together they can produce response, yet apart from these two there is no resonance.
Since both [types of] existence can be spoken of as being transcended, and because the four attachments are taught according to the capacities of sentient beings,
none of the sutras or treatises discussing response and resonance (ganying) deviate from these four.

Regarding the four questions on false attachment, the first section examines the capacity [of the practitioner] from two perspectives. First, the doubt that wholesome acts performed with false attachment are not the capacity for liberation.
Question: Can wholesome acts performed with false attachment produce karmic results?
Second, the answer that false attachment is indeed evil and can produce such results.
Answer: False attachment is also capable of producing [karmic results], even though it is evil.

Second, the question concerning ordinary beings and the demonstration that the sages extricate one from the heterodox and lead one back to the orthodox.
First, the question. Question: The name "ordinary being" implies heterodoxy; thus, goodness invites pleasure while evil evokes suffering. The name "sage" implies orthodoxy;
thus, the orthodox is neither good nor evil, and neither pleasure nor suffering. How can the heterodoxy of good and evil evoke the orthodoxy that is neither good nor evil?
Yes. Second, the answer:
The answer is that the True Sage’s compassion extracts one from the deviations of both good and evil, causing one to enter the correctness that is neither good nor evil.
There is a responsive resonance.
Regarding the fourth point, "Compassion as the function for benefiting sentient beings," there are two parts; first is the heading.

Question: Are "response" (ganying) and "compassion" (cibei) identical or different? If they are identical, why can they be distinguished into two chapters: "The Fundamental Principle" (zong) and "Function" (yong)? If they are different, please explain their meaning. Answer: The methods for opening and closing the categories of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) have many established paths. Since this present text combines *prajñā* and the *dharmakāya* as the essence (*tǐ*), it then distinguishes "liberation" (*vimukti*) to establish the fundamental principle (*zong*). Thus, although response and compassion are not separate in substance, they are differentiated here according to the requirements of the exposition. Furthermore, while the essence is one, its functions are manifold; therefore, the chapter on function is established separately from the chapter on the fundamental principle. This is because the nature of compassion is to respond to conditions, whereas the nature of wisdom is to illuminate reality. Consequently, these two aspects are presented as distinct chapters. Moreover, since the fundamental principle is the primary focus, it is treated extensively, while function is secondary and thus treated concisely. This is why the chapter on the fundamental principle is extensive, while the chapter on function is brief. Finally, because the fundamental principle is the root and function is the branch, the former is placed first and the latter follows. This is the reason for the distinction between the two chapters. Furthermore, the fundamental principle is the cause, while function is the effect; the cause is the internal, while the effect is the external. Although the function is one, its virtues possess two capacities: "resonance and response" (*ganying*) refers generally to the communication between the transcendent and the mundane, while "compassion" (*cibei*) specifically clarifies the bestowing of salvation through both giving and extracting from suffering.
If one were to discuss resonance and response without mentioning compassion, it would be like a benevolent king descending to the world without the merit of governing.
Now, by clarifying resonance and response, the meaning of the entire scripture is fully encompassed; therefore, this is established as the second principle.
Showing compassion fulfills the purpose of benefiting sentient beings; therefore, it is established as the "function. To open the one into two is intended in this brief manner.

Second, regarding the two types of wisdom (jñāna), the explanation of the two begins with the formal discussion of the implicit and the explicit. First, a brief exposition, which consists of two parts corresponding to the two [types of wisdom]. First, the correspondence to the two.

Second, the answer.

This response addresses two types of wisdom; while the general discourse applies to both, this specific passage is attached to the text to clearly elucidate the benefits of manifesting and concealing, and thus it should be applied accordingly.

The function of the two wisdoms extends throughout both sections, as they are fully endowed with wisdom, compassion, and skillful means; this present chapter, however, explains their specific functions.
Second, regarding the interpretation by others, the following section clarifies the benefits based on the two bodies. First, it presents the limited explanations of others.

He [the Master] explained that the Dharma-body benefits beings through its profound mystery and is therefore eternal, while the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) appears briefly and then disappears, and is therefore impermanent.
Second, "Now, to clarify" below clarifies the current correct meaning. This has two parts: first, the Dharma; second, the initial clarification that both bodies are eternal.
First, the initial clarification that both bodies are eternal.

Now, it is clear that the Dharma-body is eternally quiescent yet constantly illuminating; this principle is necessarily so. The Response-body benefits beings everywhere without ever ceasing or failing, which is likewise the meaning of "eternal.
The Dharma is eternal by virtue of its quiescence and illumination; the Response is eternal by virtue of its uninterrupted activity.
Second, "If one says... and below clarifies that both bodies possess both benefits and lack thereof.
If one says there are [benefits], they should not be considered impermanent; for the Dharma-body likewise possesses both benefit and lack of benefit.
Second, "Therefore, one knows... and below clarifies that these two benefits are non-dual and without distinction.
Therefore, one should know that both are eternal and both are impermanent; both possess the hidden and the manifest, like the sun and moon illuminating together, one waning while the other waxes.

Because the Tathāgata constantly uses these two dharmas—eternity and impermanence—to cultivate sentient beings, he speaks of the two birds flying together and calls them "the eternal" and "the impermanent."
The second is illustrated by the following analogy:
For example, just as when planting seeds, whether through external conditions such as the sun, wind, and rain, or internal factors such as the soil's vitality, warmth, and moisture,
all things flourish and receive benefit both in their hidden potential and their manifest form— so too is it with this.
Second, "herein below" refers to the extensive explanation.

Herein, one should employ the tenfold refutation of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) by means of the King Samādhi to distinguish the instruments for benefiting sentient beings through compassion;
these are all contained within the profound sections of the *Daoben* (Great Root).
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies the twenty-five kings of samādhi, which destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) and reveal the true, eternal nature of the self (*ātman*).
This passage generally contains four intentions: first, to bring forth the faults and afflictions of all states of existence; second, to clarify the merits of the fundamental dharma;

third, to conclude by establishing the accomplishment of samādhi through practice; and fourth, to demonstrate how Avalokiteśvara, through his own practice of compassion, has already destroyed the delusions, karma, and afflictions of all states of existence.
The fact that the patient has already accomplished the samādhi of merit is precisely because he uses compassion to cause others to shatter existence;
thus, it is known that the present application corresponds to the fourth intention.

Second, the question regarding the contemplation below simultaneously elucidates both the fundamental and the manifested aspects. First, clarifying that the fundamental and the manifested are difficult to know. First, the question.
Question: Since Avalokiteśvara’s benefit of sentient beings is so vast, is he already a Buddha or still a bodhisattva?
Answer: His original ground is difficult to know, yet the sūtra contains two accounts.

as the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* clarifies, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta attained the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) and travel back and forth throughout the ten directions to transform sentient beings.
In the past, under the Tathāgata Golden Light Lion’s Play (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa-siṃhavikrīḍita*), there was a king named Majestic Virtue (*Tejodhipati*).

Fifth, regarding the clarification of the scriptural characteristics: the categories of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtras are numerous;

they differ according to whether they concern the Requesting of Avalokiteśvara, the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara, the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara, the Repentance of Avalokiteśvara, or the Great Compassionate and Heroic Avalokiteśvara.
Second, the present section below demonstrates what has been transmitted. First, it demonstrates one chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
What is transmitted here is precisely one chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, consisting of one thousand five hundred and thirty words.
Second, the subsequent section clarifies the reasons for the distinct transmission.
As for this distinct transmission, it was the Dharma Master Dharmarakṣa—also known as the Bodhisattva Īśvara—who traveled through the Pamirs to arrive in Hexi.
There, the King of Hexi, Juqu Mengxun, took refuge in the True Dharma and possessed [the means to support it].
He informed the Dharma Master of his ailment, whereupon the Master said, "Avalokiteśvara has a karmic affinity with this land;

therefore, have him recite [the name], and the suffering of his illness will immediately be removed. Consequently, this was transmitted separately as one chapter and circulated outside the main body of the canon.

Second, this section below clarifies the characteristics of the teaching. First, it is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the characteristic of the *amṛta* (the finest essence). First, it clarifies the intent of this chapter:

since this chapter belongs to the "Circulation" (*pratyāmnāya*) section of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it serves to universally propagate the teaching that reveals the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional, thereby causing the implicit and explicit meanings to harmonize.
The dual benefit extends into the future; by means of bodies corresponding to the ten dharma-realms, he perfectly responds to all beings to bring them to liberation.

Regarding the "opening of the provisional and revealing the real," this refers for now to the section on the Trace Gate (*jimen*); one should further say it is the "opening of the trace and revealing the fundamental" (*kaiji xianben*).
This [section], from the "Expedient Means" chapter (*fangbian pin*) up to the nineteenth verse of the "Distinguishing Merits" chapter (*fenbie gongde pin*), constitutes the main body of the teaching.

The Master [Zhiyi] considers the nineteen verses that follow to constitute both the gate of the manifested trace (*jiben*) and the gate of the original source (*benji*), serving as the text for circulation.

Second, regarding "the person of the Perfect [Vehicle]" (*yuanren*) and below, this clarifies the flavor of the teaching. Since the person of the Perfect Vehicle upholds the Perfect Dharma and elucidates this Perfect Teaching, it constitutes the aspect of circulating the Perfect Teaching.
To establish the discourse through the five flavors is precisely to circulate the flavor of *amṛta* (the finest essence).

The "perfect Dharma" refers to the teachings elucidated by the two gates of the original and the trace; the "Perfect Teaching" refers to the teachings that elucidate these two gates of the original and the trace.
Section Two: Examining the Meaning of the Opening of the Doctrine of Bestowal in the Latter Part of the Text. Part One: Examining the Formation of the Provisional Characteristics of Bestowal.
Sub-part One: Questioning Based on the Discrepancy between Expedient Means and Perfection.
The text of the question states: "The power of expedient means is diverse and not uniform; the teachings should likewise differ. How can this be the Perfect Teaching?"
The characteristics.

Second, the answer concerning the lower [teachings] by way of establishing provisional means based on the ultimate reality. This has two parts: first, the answer establishing provisional means based on the ultimate person; second, the answer establishing provisional means based on the person who speaks.

Regarding the former: although the capacities of those to be taught throughout the Dharma-realm are not [identical], [the Buddha] expounds the Perfect Teaching in its full breadth to act as a universal guide for those with such capacities.

One must not allow those who uphold the Dharma to act arbitrarily or with partiality; for example, although the Buddha taught the One Vehicle, he distinguished it by speaking of three vehicles—how could one then claim that the Buddha was himself a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha?

The Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) specifically explains this as a means to attract those with gradual capacities; how could it be that because the Buddha preached the Small Vehicle, he himself would be considered "small," or that the person who can preach it would be categorized as belonging to the Perfect Teaching?
Second, regarding the "bestowal" [of the teaching], the answer is that by relying on the provisional, one can penetrate the real.
Furthermore, the entrustment states: "If there are those who have deep faith and understanding, preach this sutra for them;

if there are those who do not believe, instruct, benefit, and gladden them with other profound teachings. Thus, while following the Buddha’s mandate to skillfully accommodate the myriad capacities of sentient beings—despite their various differences—it is solely for the purpose of circulating the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Regarding those who possess deep faith and understanding, he entrusts them by saying that those who believe in the Tathāgata’s wisdom are [the true followers], whereas those who do not believe are the people of the seven expedient means (*saptopāya*).

Second, in the passage beginning with "Again he asks," there is an examination establishing the characteristics of the opening of the provisional (*upāya-kauśalya*). This has two parts: first, the objection based on the commonality of the capacities of the audience at the Deer Park.

He asked again: "If the person who can preach is perfected in the teaching and also perfected in practice, yet the capacities of the people to whom they preach differ, what teaching does this person receive?
If they receive a partial teaching, they would be the same as those at the Deer Park; if they receive a perfect teaching, their capacities should likewise be identical."
Regarding the statement that although the person who received [the teaching] was perfect, the teaching itself was provisional and small—just as at the Deer Park, was the Buddha not indeed perfect?
It is simply judged as belonging to the Tripitaka based on the recipient; how could it be otherwise here?
Second, this is the answer concerning the opening of the provisional through the traces of the various schools.
Answer: In the past at the Deer Park, before the Buddha had yet revealed his fundamental nature, his manifested traces did not coincide with the three refuges;

thus, for a single person, the Dharma they received was not yet perfected, and the provisional teachings they followed could not be called "perfect. Now, this sutra has already opened up and revealed both the provisional and the real: although there are various bodies, their fundamental and manifested aspects are inconceivably one;
and although various dharmas are taught, it is for the purpose of opening the way to the Perfect Path, so there is no fault in the meaning.

In the Āgamas and the Minor Collection (Kṣudraka), the provisional traces have not yet been revealed, so that the flavor of the teaching remains categorized as "Small" according to the capacities of beings.

Now, this sutra reveals and clarifies that the provisional is itself the real, and the trace is itself the source. Although it speaks of "small" teachings, it is a universal and perfect sutra; how could it be the same as [the teachings of] the Deer Park?

Section Three: Questions on the Superior and Inferior to Examine the Formation of the Phase of Sublime Function. Part One: Questions Concerning the Discrepancy between the Phase of Abandonment and the Phase of Function.
Question: The preceding text states, "Directly abandoning expedient means," yet here it says, "by means of expedient means. Why is this?
Second, the answer concerning the inconceivability of essence and function:
In the previous [passage], because it was intended to manifest the reality (*tattva*), it said "abandoning"; here, because the discussion concerns function, it says "manifesting.
Thus, the inconceivability of essence and function is one.

The True Teaching (Zhengzong) discards the provisional to establish the real; therefore, it speaks of abandoning the circulation [of the provisional] for the sake of the real. Because the provisional was established for the sake of the real, one must employ it to manifest the reality.
To discuss the provisional function after the reality has been revealed is precisely the secret and subtle skillful means of this present sutra.
